"So on one island the birds might end up with one shape, and on another island, different food, different shape," Eleanor said, already writing. "Same birds, different islands." She copied her frog numbers into a new column and titled the poster with a question instead of an answer, because that was what a real scientist would conserve: every measurement, even the boring ones, in case the pattern was still hiding.

The pond smelled of algae and wet wood, and somewhere a green frog began to croak. Eleanor capped her pen and said, "Same time next week?"

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah reader follows the words with a yad, a pointer whose name means hand, so that the parchment itself is not touched.
story:
The sanctuary smelled of dust and old wood, and the afternoon light came through the tall windows in long stripes that reached almost to the bimah. Thomas stood at the table where the Torah scroll lay open, its parchment pale and crowded with dark letters that had no vowels and no spaces between the sentences. His bar mitzvah was in five weeks, and he had to read four verses out loud, in Hebrew, in front of everyone. He had the words half memorized already. The reading was not the problem. The problem was that every time he practiced, his eyes slid off the line like his sneakers on wet pavement.

"Again," said Ms. Wilson, the woman from the congregation who had offered to coach him on Sundays. She was small and quick, with reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, and she wanted this hour for herself as much as for him, because her own grandson lived far away and she liked having a student in the building again. "From the second verse."

Thomas leaned closer. The letters were beautiful up close, faintly raised, the ink gone slightly brown at the edges of the crowns. Without thinking, he reached out his index finger and set it down on the parchment under the line he was reading, the way he would track a line in a textbook. "Vayomer el," he began.

Ms. Wilson took his wrist, not roughly, and lifted his hand away. Then she picked up a slim silver rod, about as long as a pencil, with a tiny closed fist at one end, and pressed it into his palm. "A yad," she said. "It means hand."

Thomas curled his fingers around it. The metal was cool and heavier than it looked. The little fist at the tip had one bent finger, like it was knocking on a door. He tried the verse again, resting the fist on the line instead of his own finger, and something unexpected happened: the letters stopped sliding. His eyes stayed pinned to wherever the silver hand pointed.

He tested it, because he did not quite believe it. He read one line following the yad, then one line with nothing at all, then one line with the yad again. Without the pointer he lost his place twice and guessed at a word. With it, he read clean through, even the tricky phrase he always fumbled. It was as if his eyes needed somewhere to land. He thought about his own hand, how touching the parchment was like a bare footprint in fresh snow, invasive, leaving a mark that could not be undone, and he was glad there was a tool for keeping his place without leaving anything behind.

The irony was not lost on him that a hand made of silver was better at this than his actual hand. He said so, and Ms. Wilson laughed, a short sound that echoed in the empty sanctuary.

At the next practice, his friend Lachlan came along to watch, mostly because there was a chess club meeting afterward and he wanted to borrow the room. Lachlan mimicked Thomas's chanting from a pew, waving an imaginary pointer with great drama, until Thomas broke off mid-verse, laughing.

"Stop it, you're going to make me lose my place."

"Impossible," Lachlan said. "You've got your robot hand."

Thomas looked down at the yad resting on the parchment, the little silver fist holding its spot on the line, patient as a held breath. He found the next word and began again.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a straight sloping line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
story:
Elizabeth had a bet going with Carolina: whoever's marble rolled fastest down the lab ramp got the last of the sour gummy worms. That meant measuring speed, which was exactly what Mr. Anderson had written on the board in his croaky handwriting: roll a ball, measure the distance, time it, then graph it.

Alycia wanted the job of timer, and she guarded the stopwatch like it was made of gold. "I've been practicing my thumb speed all week," she said, clicking it three times to prove it. Elizabeth marked the floor with tape at every meter and rolled a steel ball down the ramp onto the smooth tiles, calling out as it crossed each mark so Alycia could catch the times.

The first graph came out wrong. The points scattered everywhere, and the line Elizabeth drew through them looked like a mountain range, not a line at all. "The ball sped up and slowed down," Carolina said, frowning at the paper. Elizabeth suspected something they couldn't see, a hidden cause, and she wondered about it while taping down a loose edge of the ramp. The ball had wobbled at the bottom, bumping onto a ridge where two tiles met. She pressed the ramp lower so the ball would land flat, then rolled again. Her scraped palm, the one she'd gotten in gym class, stung under its bandage, and her mom had said to keep it covered to prevent an infection, so she rolled with her left hand instead.

This time the points lined up almost perfectly. One meter in one second, two meters in two seconds, three in three. When she connected them with her ruler, the line went up the graph straight and even, like a staircase rail. "Look at that," she said. Carolina leaned over. Elizabeth tapped the paper. "A straight sloping line means it's moving at a constant speed. The ball didn't speed up or slow down at all. It just kept going the same." Carolina squinted at it, then grinned and rolled her own ball down the ramp.

Carolina's graph came out straight too, but her line climbed less steeply than Elizabeth's. So Carolina's ball traveled a shorter distance in the same time, which meant it was slower, and the gummy worms were Elizabeth's. She folded the graph carefully to preserve it, wanting it exact and unwrinkled for Monday, when Mr. Anderson put graphs up on the board. The bell was imminent, ringing in less than a minute, and Alycia clicked the stopwatch one last time. "Four seconds exactly," she announced, "to clean up." Elizabeth slid the steel ball into her pocket.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope.
story:
Quinn crouched at the edge of the pond with a jar in one hand and a plastic knife in the other, wondering, not for the first time, why she had promised Mckenna an onion. "For the microscope, obviously," Mckenna had said at lunch, as though onions were the most natural thing in the world to carry to a pond. "Mr. Morningstar said we could borrow the field scope if we brought our own specimen. Eunice is bringing the slides."

Mr. Morningstar was already there on the flat rock by the reeds, setting up the little portable microscope with its mirror tilted toward the sun. He taught sixth grade science and kept bees on weekends, and he had a way of standing very still, as if any sudden movement might frighten off a discovery. "You know," he said, "when I was twelve, I once tried to look at a rock through a microscope for an entire afternoon. I was convinced there was something in there."

"And was there?" Quinn asked.

"There was not. But I learned more from that rock than from a dozen good slides." He laughed at himself, which Quinn liked, because some adults would rather face extinction than admit a mistake. The pond bugs skated past in the shallows while he clipped a blank slide to the stage.

Quinn had cut her onion chunk the night before, a fat wedge right through the middle, because she had figured a big piece would show more. She pared a slice off it now, laid it on the slide, and pressed her eye to the lens. Darkness. Not dimness, but pure black, as though the microscope had been switched off, which it could not be, because it had no switch. She pulled back, checked the mirror, tried again. Still nothing.

"Let me guess," Eunice said, arriving with a box of slides and cover slips and the smug look of someone who had read ahead in the textbook. "You cut it thick, didn't you." She said it lightly, but Quinn heard the edge of it anyway, the small beginnings of a ridicule she'd have to decide whether to care about later.

Quinn sat back on her heels and thought about the pond water. When she scooped a jar of it and held it up, she could see through it, could see her own fingers wobbling on the other side. When she scooped up a jar of mud, she could see nothing at all. The mud was thick; the water was thin. Light got through thin things and got stopped by thick ones. And the microscope needed light, that was the whole point of the little mirror. She picked up the onion wedge again and turned it in her fingers, peeling away the thick outer layers until she found the papery inner skin, so delicate it tore when she breathed on it. She peeled off a piece no bigger than a fingernail, laid it flat in a drop of pond water, and lowered the cover slip.

"Whoa," she said. Then, louder, "Whoa, come look." Under the lens the skin had broken into rows and rows of separate bricks, each one walled off from the next, with a dark dot sitting in the middle of every single cell like a seed in a jelly. It was one cell thick, that flimsy inner skin, and the light went straight through it. Mr. Morningstar leaned in, made a low humming sound of approval, and handed her a pencil. "Label the outer edge of each brick the cell wall," he said. "The dark dot is the nucleus."

Mckenna took her turn at the eyepiece and pronounced it, with great objective certainty, "the most disgusting beautiful thing I have ever seen." Quinn drew the bricks slowly and carefully, thinking about Mr. Morningstar's useless rock, and decided she did not mind Eunice's teasing after all, since it had been the black slide, not the book, that had taught her.

"Tomorrow," Quinn said, "I'm bringing celery."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
Ryan had lost the spelling bee at the community center last year on the word "accumulate," and he had spent a whole week afterward rereading the word list, five times a night, until his eyes ached. When the new list arrived in January, he stared at it in the gym hallway and felt his stomach knot. Rereading had not worked before, and he could not figure out why, because he had honestly tried.

In the library, his friend Warren was reading over his shoulder. "You're just staring at the list again? You did that last year."

"I know," Ryan said. "That's the problem."

Axel slid into the seat across from them and dumped out a handful of flash cards. "My sister made these for her biology test. She says covering the answers and guessing out loud works better than reading the chapter twice. Something about guessing being hard at first, then getting better."

That night, Ryan handed the list to his dad. "Don't let me look. Just ask me the words, and if I get one wrong, tell me, and I'll try it again tomorrow." The first evening was rough. He missed "conscientious" three separate times, and he missed "raspberry," which was embarrassing. But the next night, he spelled both of them correctly on the first try, and the night after that too. The improvement felt gradual, but it was definitely there, like a path getting easier to walk each time.

He wanted to know if this was a real thing or just luck, so he searched on the library computer and found it. A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it. He read the sentence twice, then leaned over to Warren. "Look at this. A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke. Testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than just rereading it. So that's why last year didn't work. I reread the list a million times and never once made myself spell anything cold."

"That's why my flash cards worked," Axel said. "I was actually testing myself. I thought I was just being lazy about reading."

On Friday, Warren left a note in Ryan's locker, folded into a paper triangle:

"Dear Ryan, I made a score chart for us. Every night this week I'm going to quiz you over the phone and mark how many you get right out of twenty. It's a ratio, gets right out of tries, so we can watch your numbers climb. If you beat tonight's score by Saturday, I owe you a pretzel. Also I'm doing the same thing with my multiplication tables so we can both demonstrate that this works. Your friend, Warren."

The phone quizzes became a habit. Monday Ryan got thirteen out of twenty. Wednesday, sixteen. Friday, nineteen, and Warren's voice crackled through the speaker: "Nineteen! That's a pretzel, and I'm paying up tomorrow."

Saturday morning, the community center gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn. Rows of folding chairs held parents, and Mr. Wang, who ran the center, stood at the microphone calling out words. Ryan sat between Axel and a girl from another school, his knee bouncing until Axel pressed a hand down on it and grinned.

"Achievement," Mr. Wang said to another speller, who misspelled it. Then it was Ryan's turn. "Conscientious," Mr. Wang said.

The word that had tripped him three times in one night now felt solid, like a stone in his hand. "C-O-N-S-C-I-E-N-T-I-O-U-S," Ryan said.

"Correct," said Mr. Wang, and Ryan walked back to his seat trying not to smile too wide.

He placed third overall, going out in round nine on "silhouette," which he would absolutely practice with Warren's flash card method that night. In the hallway afterward, his dad shook his hand like a coach, and Warren held out a warm pretzel in a paper sleeve. "A deal's a deal," Warren said. "Now eat it before round ten starts in your stomach."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A break statement stops a loop immediately, so a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Lakebirch smelled like sunscreen and burnt popcorn, and Lucy had claimed the keyboard by the window so she could watch the canoe dock while her program ran. Her project was due before the camp talent show on Friday: a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. She had typed the whole thing in one afternoon, which she considered heroic, except for one small problem. When she entered 51, the screen filled with the words "not prime" over and over, line after line, like the program was trying to irritate her personally.

"Fifty lines," said Ricky, leaning over her shoulder. "It printed 'not prime' fifty times. I counted, because clearly I have no life." Behind him, Miles held up his phone with a picture of the screen, which he had titled "The World's Most Convinced Computer."

"It checks every number from 2 up to fifty," Lucy said, mostly to herself. She traced the loop with her finger on the screen. "So every single time it doesn't divide evenly, it prints 'not prime.' Three doesn't divide it, print. Four doesn't divide it, print. It just keeps going." The moment she said it out loud, the hidden shape of the bug appeared, clear as a jellyfish in shallow water. "It already found that three goes into fifty-one. Why is it still talking?"

"You could ask it nicely to stop," Miles offered. "Computers love that."

Lucy flipped through her notes from Monday's session until she found a line Ms. Castillo had written on the whiteboard before canoe practice: break. She had copied it down without really looking at it, the way you copy a word in a language you don't speak yet. Now she dropped a break under the line that printed "not prime," so the moment the program found one divisor, it would quit the loop right there and move on to the rest of the program. She saved the file, held her breath, and typed 51.

The screen said "not prime" once. Then it said goodbye and waited politely for the next number.

"ONE line," Ricky announced, holding up a single finger like a referee. "That's not a program, that's an organism with manners." Lucy entered 97, and the screen said "prime," which felt like the computer was complimenting her. She entered 2, then 49, then her cabin number, just to watch it decide.

Ms. Castillo wandered past on her way to the dock and read the screen upside down, an apparently hereditary teacher skill. "Nice break statement," she said.

"Thanks," said Lucy. "It took fifty tries to find it." She typed 1000003 and pressed enter.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
Aaron had exactly forty minutes to get signed out of the doctor's office and across town to the audition, and the waiting room clock seemed to have developed a personal grudge against him. Lyric sat beside him, flipping through a magazine about fishing, which he had no interest in, purely to have something to hold.

"You're breathing weird," Lyric said without looking up.

"I'm breathing normal."

"You're breathing like a golden retriever in July."

The truth was that Aaron's heart was pounding, hard, the way it did before solos, and his breath kept coming fast even though he was sitting perfectly still. Nothing here was dangerous. The worst thing in the room was a poster about eating vegetables. So why was his body acting like he'd been chased into the office by wolves? He had a theory forming, but he needed data.

"Aaron," the nurse called. In the exam room she wrapped the cuff around his arm, then pressed two fingers to his wrist and frowned. "Pulse is up. Any reason?"

"Is that adrenaline?" Aaron asked. "From, you know, the adrenal glands?"

"It could be," the nurse said, writing on her chart. "Fight-or-flight. When it kicks in, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing speed up."

So that was it. His brain, apparently, had decided that a middle-school audition counted as an emergency, and it had sent the signal without asking him. He tested the idea right there. He slowed his breathing on purpose, long inhale, longer exhale, the coping trick his mom had shown him after the incident at the recital. After a minute, the nurse checked his pulse again and raised an eyebrow at the drop. It wasn't magic. It was just a lever he could actually reach.

Mr. Bighorn came in, looked at the chart, looked at Aaron, and said, "You're here for the physical form for the show, aren't you. The one that's due today."

"Yes. It was inevitable that I'd end up here eventually. I put it off until it was a crisis."

Mr. Bighorn signed the form without ceremony, which Aaron felt was the finest medical care he had ever received. Then the doctor paused, pen still hovering. "One more thing. Your friend in the waiting room, the one telling the receptionist that you absolutely cannot leave yet. Is something going on there?"

Aaron went cold. Lyric. Lyric, whose mom had said no to the audition unless he finished his physical too, and whose physical was not scheduled, ever, in any foreseeable future. Lyric, who had contributed the fishing magazine and the encouragement and the ride, and apparently also the delay, because if Aaron missed the audition, Lyric could miss it too and blame someone else.

Aaron walked out into the waiting room and held up the signed form like a verdict. "Nice try. You have ten minutes to call your mom and tell her you're coming, or I'm doing my solo and telling the director you choked."

Lyric set down the magazine with great dignity. "For the record, that was a strategy."

"For the record, my stress level was a medical event."

They ran for the door, and behind them the clock hit 3:22.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
story:
At Addyson's house the rain hammered the windows so hard it sounded like gravel being dumped on the roof, and Addyson's phone would not stop buzzing. "Look at this," she said, holding it out. "Somebody posted that the creek by school is flooding and the bridge is already under water. Everybody's sharing it." Jade leaned closer. The photo showed brown water swallowing a metal railing, with a stop sign poking out of the current like a flag. It looked exactly like the bridge they crossed every morning.

Dominique, who had come over to wait out the storm, grabbed her shoes. "My brother walks that way home. If the bridge is out he'd try to cross anyway. He's totally impulsive, he'd wade right in." She was halfway to the door when Jade caught her sleeve. "Wait. Who posted it first?" Addyson scrolled, shrugging. "I don't know. It just showed up. It has like two hundred shares already." The number was climbing as they watched, which somehow made Jade feel worse, not better.

Something about the photo kept snagging on her. The trees in the background were bright green and heavy with leaves, but it was only March, and every tree she'd seen that week was bare and dripping. "That doesn't generate a whole lot of confidence," she muttered, mostly to herself. Addyson frowned. "What do you mean?" Jade pulled out her own phone. "My mom showed me this once. You can do a reverse image search. You give it the picture instead of words, and it shows you everywhere that photo appeared online before." She dragged the flood photo into the search bar, and the three of them huddled over the small screen while the rain drummed on.

The results loaded slowly. Jade held her breath without meaning to. First a row of grey boxes, then, one by one, the images appeared, and every single one of them was the same photo. The same stop sign. The same railing. A news story from another state, and the date on it was from years earlier, before any of them had even started middle school. "It's old," Jade whispered. "It's an old picture being passed off as new." Addyson scrolled back to the post, and its two hundred shares had become four hundred. "People are going to keep sending it," she said. "Half the grade is going to think the bridge is gone."

Dominique was already typing a message to her brother, thumbs flying, and Jade started a reply to the original post with the link to the older story attached. "Somebody has to say something," she said, "before my mom sees it and has a monopoly on panicking." Addyson laughed for the first time in twenty minutes and hit send. Outside, the rain finally began to slacken, and Dominique's phone chimed with one word from her brother: "Dry."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
story:
Ethan stood in line at the French pavilion with his festival passport open in one hand. The booth had two symmetrical banners, red and blue, hung on either side of a small table where a boy about Ethan's age was stamping papers. Every visitor had to describe their family and pets in full French sentences before earning the stamp, and Ethan had practiced exactly four sentences on the bus.

"Bonjour," the boy said. "Je m'appelle Arnaud. Et toi?"

"Je m'appelle Ethan," Ethan said. Then he went for it. "J'habite avec ma mère et mon père. J'ai un chien et deux chats. Je suis treze ans."

Arnaud tilted his head. "Treize ans?"

"Treize. Treize ans," Ethan repeated. "Je suis treize ans."

Arnaud shook his head and held up both hands. "Non. On dit 'J'ai treize ans.'" He tapped the stamp on the table without using it. "'J'ai' means 'I have.' 'J'ai treize ans' means 'I am thirteen,' but word for word it says 'I have thirteen years.'"

Ethan stared at him. "You have thirteen years? Like the years belong to you?"

"Oui," Arnaud said, grinning. "They're yours."

Behind Ethan, a girl from his school, Milla, leaned around him. "Wait, seriously? I've been telling everyone 'Je suis douze ans' all morning." She looked at her own passport, where a booth volunteer had written something in the margin. "No wonder she kept correcting me."

Ethan stepped out of the line to think. So French used avoir, to have, for age, instead of être, to be. That was the pattern, and he wanted to know whether it held everywhere or only sometimes. He wrote two test sentences on the back of his passport: one with avoir, one with être. Then he tried a different question. If age worked like possession, maybe he could say he had his years the same way he had his dog.

He got back in line, and when Arnaud waved him forward, Ethan held up the paper. "J'ai treize ans," he said. "Et j'ai un chien. Le chien a quatre ans."

Arnaud laughed and slammed the stamp down. "Parfait!" A small motion sensor above the table blinked the lamp on as Ethan reached for the page. He pressed his thumb over the ink, which had started to contract into a tight ring on the paper, and Milla leaned over his shoulder to read his sentences.

"Say the dog one again," she said. "Slow. I'm stealing that for the Spanish booth, they probably do it too."

"Tu as raison," Ethan said, and walked with her toward the next line.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
story:
Emma's little brother had left his empty cereal bowl on the keyboard again, which was almost the least of her problems. The real problem was the message waiting on the screen from Jaya, sent an hour ago: "Did you see what Juniper posted? She says the school is canceling the fall concert forever. Is that true?"

Emma slumped into the desk chair and clicked through to the post. There it was, in Juniper's usual giant letters: FALL CONCERT CANCELED FOREVER. SPREAD THE WORD. Underneath, forty kids had already replied with crying faces and angry faces, and someone had started a petition.

She typed back to Jaya: "Hold on. I'm checking." It felt strange to type that, because checking was exactly the thing nobody else seemed to be doing. But last week at dinner, when her brother had shouted "spinach is disgusting" and she had answered "no, it's a vegetable," their mom had laughed and pointed out that one of them was stating a taste and the other was saying something that could actually be proven true or false. A fact could be tested against evidence, her mom had said, while an opinion was just what someone believed or felt, and no amount of evidence could prove it one way or the other. That argument had ended with her brother grudgingly eating his spinach, but the idea had stuck with Emma like a burr.

She messaged Juniper directly. "Where did you hear the concert is canceled forever?"

Juniper replied fast. "Mr. García told my cousin that the gym is booked for something in October."

Emma read that twice. A booking in October was not the same thing as forever. It might even be temporary, a one-time conflict, the kind of thing that got moved. She tried to think of how to test it. Evidence, she thought. What would count as evidence? A schedule. A person who actually knew.

She opened the school website and found the events calendar. October 18 was marked "Gym reserved: Regional Artisans' Fair." An artisan, she remembered from Mr. García's vocabulary list, was a person who made things by hand, and apparently a whole fair of them needed the gym. She scrolled to November. There, in green letters: Fall Concert, November 15.

Her fingers flew. She copied the link, pasted it into Juniper's thread, and wrote: "The concert isn't canceled. The gym has the Artisans' Fair in October, and the concert is November 15. It's on the official calendar."

The replies changed fast. Some kids apologized to Juniper, and one wrote "fake news!" which Emma thought was unfair, since Juniper hadn't lied on purpose. Juniper herself sent a private message: "My cousin said 'the concert's off for October.' I guess I turned that into forever. Sorry."

"It's okay," Emma typed. "You had an opinion about it, kind of. But it was also a claim someone could check, and when I checked, the evidence refuted it. That's all."

There was a pause, then Juniper answered with a single line: "Next time check first, spread word second."

"Deal," Emma wrote, and closed the thread just as Jaya's new message popped up: "You're my hero. Want to come over and practice our duet?"

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
story:
Ryan had read the last page of "The Lottery" three times, and it still felt like the story had tricked him. Now Ms. Krause was telling the book club to flip back to the first paragraph, and Ryan was pretty sure he did not want to see it again.

"Ryan, why don't you read it out loud," said Destiny, grinning, because she knew he hated reading out loud.

He read it anyway. Kids gathering in the square, flowers, sunshine, a warm summer day. And there, in the middle of all that calm, Bobby Martin had a pocket full of stones, and the other children were piling up stones in a corner. Ryan stopped. "Wait. Stones. Why would she even mention stones if they're just, like, playing?"

"To dismiss it as kids being kids," said Jennifer. "That's what I did. Kids love rocks. You put a rock in your pocket, you're a normal kid."

Ms. Krause tilted her hand like, go on. Ryan flipped to the end, then back again, like he was bouncing between two rooms in the same house. "At the end they use the stones. On the person who wins the lottery." He tapped the page. "So the first paragraph already told us. She snuck it in while we were busy looking at the flowers."

"So the opening paragraph isn't neutral at all," Destiny said slowly. "It looks neutral. It's wearing a neutral costume."

"Like a prism," Ryan said. "It looks clear until the light goes through, and then suddenly there's all this other stuff showing up. Except backwards. The stuff was there the whole time and only shows up at the end."

Jennifer squinted at him. "That metaphor needs work."

"Metaphors need work," Ryan agreed, "that's why they're metaphors."

Ms. Krause asked what the stones suggested, and Ryan said it plainly: that something bad was coming, and the town was used to it, because the kids were collecting stones like it was a chore, like kids setting the table for dinner. The whole club went quiet for a second, the way it does when someone says the true thing.

"Shirley Jackson published this in The New Yorker," Ms. Krause said, "back in 1948." She let that sit there. "People wrote angry letters. They said she had cheated."

"She didn't cheat," said Ryan. "She told us everything on page one. We just didn't want to look at the stones." He held the story up like evidence. "I'm rereading everything now. Every bird, every hat, every sandwich."

"Good luck with the sandwiches," said Destiny. "Some sandwiches are just sandwiches."

"None of them are just sandwiches anymore," Ryan said, and turned back to page one.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
Anthony spread three bean plants across the folding table at the edge of the school gymnasium, where Ms. Berg had set up the science fair stations in two parallel rows. His poster read "Does fertilizer make beans grow faster?" and two of his plants proved it, he thought. The fertilized one stood tall and the plain-water one stood small. But something bothered him, and he rolled it around in his mind while he straightened his measuring stick.

"You look like you're doing math in your head," said Harley, who was setting up a volcano at the next table. "That's scary."

"I watered them the same and gave them the same light," Anthony said slowly. "But what if the small one was always going to be small? Like, what if it was just a wimpy seed from the start?" He tapped the pot with the shorter plant. "How would I know the fertilizer did anything, if I can't see what it would have done anyway?"

Harley shrugged and went back to his baking soda. Mikayla wandered over from the sign-in table, chewing the end of a pencil, and listened to Anthony explain the problem. "So you want to know what the plant does with nothing done to it," she said. "Like, a normal one. A regular one."

"A what?" Anthony asked, and then he stopped, because a word he had half-heard somewhere drifted up. He tried it out. "A control group?" Mikayla nodded like the word had a smell she recognized. "My cousin did one. A control group gets no change at all. You don't water it extra, you don't feed it, nothing. Then you've got it to compare the tested ones against." Anthony stared at his two pots and thought about it. "So I needed one more plant. Plain water, no fertilizer, same everything else. Then if the fertilized one beats both of them, the fertilizer really did it."

He didn't have a third plant, so he did what he could. He wrote it on his poster in marker: "Control group: gets no change at all, no fertilizer. Baseline to compare against." Ms. Berg paused at his table on her rounds, read the line, and raised an eyebrow at him. "Next year?" she said. Anthony promised to comply with proper procedure next year, and she moved on, though she came back twice more to look at his beans, which he decided to take as a good sign.

When the judges came by, one of them, a man with a clipboard, asked Anthony what he would do differently. Anthony pointed at the gap where a third pot should have stood. "I'd add a plant that gets nothing done to it," he said. "Then I'd know if I was really measuring the fertilizer, or just measuring a lucky seed."

"Good answer," the judge said, and made a mark on his clipboard.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: In his 'Rhetoric', Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, reasoning and evidence.
story:
Carson had promised Mr. Ortiz he would have a debate case ready by Monday, and the only quiet place to build one was his grandpa's house, where the porch smelled like cedar and old lemon drops. His topic was "Schools should ban homework over weekends." He knew what he thought. He just didn't know how to make anyone else think it too.

"So what do you actually have?" asked Rayna, who had biked over with a notebook wedged in her backpack next to a squashed granola bar. She flopped into the porch swing and held out her hand for his notes.

Carson read her his first point. "Weekend homework makes kids exhausted. My cousin was up until midnight on Sunday and fell asleep in math class."

Rayna winced. "That's a sad story. It's just one kid. My sister had a whole weekend with no homework and she was still lethargic on Mondays, so one story doesn't prove anything." She tapped her pen against the swing chain. "You need numbers. Briar's team has numbers. They polled like a hundred students."

Carson sat on the porch steps and stared at the garden, where his grandpa's gnomes stood guard over the tomatoes like a tiny silent jury. He remembered Mr. Ortiz mentioning an old Greek guy one time, holding up a battered book. Aristotle, in his "Rhetoric," had described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, reasoning and evidence. Carson had copied it into his notebook without really looking at it. Now he looked.

"That's it," he said. "I built my whole case on pathos. Sad cousin, midnight, tired kids. That's emotions. Briar's team has the logos part, the numbers, plus ethos because they'll say they surveyed people themselves." He jumped up. "I need all three. A claim, evidence, and a warrant for each point, so the numbers actually connect to the claim instead of just sitting there."

They spent the next hour at the porch table, racing through a stack of articles Grandpa brought out with a plate of peanut butter crackers. Carson found a survey of two thousand students, then wrote a warrant for it: if weekend homework predicts lower Monday test scores, the policy is hurting the very thing it's supposed to help. He read his new case out loud to the tomato gnomes, and even the gnomes looked convinced.

"Better," Rayna admitted. "But don't abandon the cousin story completely. Pathos counts too. Just don't lead with it."

On Monday, when Briar's team flashed their pie chart, Carson stood up with his notes and a calm, credible voice. "Our opponents showed you feelings and a chart. Let me show you how they connect, and where they don't."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: A split is the time for one section of a race; an 800-metre runner's 400-metre split shows right away whether the first lap was faster or slower than planned.
story:
The district meet was in four days, and Elliot still could not run the eight hundred metres without dying on the second lap. Every time, he sprinted the first lap like it was the only one, and every time his legs turned to rubber halfway through the second while runners passed him on the final curve. Mr. Brennan had stopped trying to correct him and simply stood at the rope with a stopwatch and a frown.

"Time trial in ten minutes," Mr. Brennan called across the gym, where cones marked a loop around the basketball courts. "Elliot, you're with Ania and Asma."

Ania stretched her hamstrings on the mats. "Don't go out ridiculous fast this time," she said. "Last week you looked like a windmill falling over."

"I can't help it," Elliot said. "Everything feels slow at the start. My legs want to go."

Asma laced her shoes. "Then you need to see it," she said. "You can't feel it, so you have to see it."

Elliot frowned. See what? He couldn't exactly watch himself run. But then Mr. Brennan mentioned he would stand at the finish line with the stopwatch, calling out the time each runner hit at the halfway point. "A split," Mr. Brennan said as he clicked the watch. "Four-hundred-metre split coming at the turn."

The whole race might hinge on that one number, Elliot realized. If his time at the halfway point was faster than he planned, it would show right there, before the race was even half over, that his first lap had been too quick. He wouldn't have to guess how he felt. He would know.

He toed the line beside Ania and Asma. "Call it loud," he said to Mr. Brennan.

The whistle blew. Elliot's legs begged to fly, but he held back, counting his steps, staying on Asma's shoulder. At the turn Mr. Brennan's voice cracked across the gym: "Elliot, sixty-two!"

Ania, breathing hard beside him, gasped, "That's still too fast, dummy, back off."

Elliot eased up. The second lap still burned, but his legs kept turning, and when he crossed the line he wasn't collapsing, he was still racing. Asma jogged over and slapped his back.

"You finished," she said. "You actually finished strong."

Mr. Brennan clicked his stopwatch and squinted at it. "Fifty-nine first lap yesterday, sixty-two today, and your total time was faster. One more trial before Thursday."

Elliot bent, hands on knees, grinning at the floor. "Line up," he said. "I want to hear that number again."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
The poster board was due in two hours, and Dylan still couldn't get the caption right. He stood in the craft room of the community centre, marker in hand, staring at the sentence he'd written about a northern explorer who had been guided by "an Inuit." Something about it bothered him, though he couldn't say what.

"Just write it and move on," said Theodore, who was gluing a strip of birchbark onto his own project across the table. "You've been on that caption forever. Nobody reads captions anyway." Theodore's board was sparse compared with Dylan's, just three photos and a hand-drawn map, and he clearly wanted to finish early so he could get to the gym before basketball open play ended.

Dylan tapped the marker against the table. He had learned, the hard way, that guessing on the small words could sink a whole project. Last year he had labelled a photo of the Haida Gwaii islands as "Hawaii" because he hadn't checked, and Mr. Ong had circled it in red pen twice. He wasn't going to guess again.

He wandered down the hall to the multipurpose room, where the weekly Inuit carving demonstration was setting up. An elderly woman was arranging soapstone figures on a cloth, and a younger man was taping up a sign that read INUKTITUT WORDS OF THE WEEK. Dylan studied the sign, which listed words like iglu and qamutik, and then, near the bottom, Inuit.

"Excuse me," Dylan said. "Is Inuit the name of the language?"

The man smiled. "The language is Inuktitut. Inuit means 'the people.'"

"One person, too?" Dylan asked.

"One person is an Inuk," the man said, straightening the sign. "Inuit, that's all of us."

Dylan felt the puzzle click into place in his head. The word he had written, "an Inuit," treated a plural word like a singular one. He tested the idea silently: if Inuit meant the people, then "guided by the Inuit" made sense, but for one guide it would have to be something else. He had been using one word for two different things without noticing.

Back in the craft room he crossed out his caption and wrote, "The explorer was guided by an Inuk hunter named in the ship's log." Theodore leaned over to read it.

"That's it? One letter change, all that worrying?"

"One letter," Dylan said, "and the right one." He set down the marker and picked up the board. In the hallway outside, the basketballs were already bouncing.
